exam: A 22‑year‑old athlete collapses during sprinting – what immediate investigations and why? — Obtain ECG and bedside echo; look for LVOT gradient and SAM; consider ICD if high‑risk features.
Explain how Valsalva differentiates HOCM from aortic stenosis. — Valsalva increases gradient in HOCM (louder murmur) but decreases it in aortic stenosis.
Patient with HOCM has persistent symptoms despite β‑blocker; what next step? — Add verapamil or disopyramide; if gradient remains ≥50 mmHg, refer for septal reduction.

What are the three major criteria for ICD implantation in HOCM? — Septal thickness ≥30 mm, family history of sudden death, unexplained syncope, NSVT on Holter, or abnormal blood pressure response to exercise.
How does anemia from malaria affect HOCM presentation? — Low preload worsens obstruction, increasing dyspnoea and syncope; treat anemia promptly.
Describe the pathophysiological basis of SAM. — Hyperdynamic contraction pulls the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum, narrowing the LVOT and causing MR.
Why are diuretics generally avoided in HOCM? — They reduce preload, further narrowing the LVOT and can precipitate syncope.
A patient from a rural clinic cannot get cardiac MRI; how do you risk‑stratify? — Use echo measurements, Holter for NSVT, family history, and symptom profile to decide on ICD.
ai.title: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A genetic disease causing asymmetric septal hypertrophy that narrows the left ventricular outflow tract. Presents with exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope and risk of sudden death.

b: Autosomal‑dominant inheritance, most commonly MYH7 or MYBPC3 mutations
Prevalence ≈1 / 500 in the general population
Obstruction defined by a peak gradient ≥30 mmHg at rest or with provocation
sections.p: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is a primary myocardial disease characterised by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, most often asymmetric septal thickening, that produces dynamic outflow obstruction.

b: Dynamic LVOT gradient rises with Valsalva, standing, or exercise
Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve contributes to obstruction and MR
Risk factors for sudden cardiac death: massive hypertrophy (≥30 mm), family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, NSVT on Holter
sections.p: The disease is a disorder of sarcomere proteins leading to myocyte disarray, fibrosis and small‑vessel disease. The obstruction is dynamic, worsening with decreased preload, afterload or increased contractility.

b: Exertional syncope suggests severe obstruction or arrhythmia
A harsh systolic ejection murmur that decreases with squatting and increases with Valsalva
Palpable sustained apical impulse due to hypertrophied septum
sections.p: Patients often present with exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, or syncope. In low‑resource settings, differential diagnoses include rheumatic mitral stenosis, anemia, and malaria‑related cardiomyopathy.

t.b: Confirms hypertrophy, measures septal thickness, and quantifies LVOT gradient; SAM and MR are visualised
Shows LV hypertrophy, deep Q waves, or arrhythmias; helps risk stratify for SCD
Detects non‑sustained ventricular tachycardia, a major SCD risk marker
Assesses extent of fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) which adds prognostic information
Provokes gradient increase and reproduces symptoms; useful when resting echo is equivocal
Identifies pathogenic sarcomere mutations; guides family screening

b: β‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) or non‑dihydropyridine calcium‑channel blockers (verapamil) to reduce heart rate and contractility
Disopyramide (if available) added for gradient reduction; avoid in patients with QT prolongation
Avoid diuretics unless volume overload, as they may worsen obstruction
Implantable cardioverter‑defibrillator (ICD) for high‑risk patients (massive hypertrophy, NSVT, family SCD)
Septal reduction therapy (surgical myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) for refractory obstruction; myectomy preferred where surgical expertise exists
sections.p: Therapy aims to relieve obstruction, control symptoms, and prevent sudden death.

b: Aortic stenosis – fixed obstruction, murmur louder with squatting, no SAM
Rheumatic mitral stenosis – diastolic murmur, history of rheumatic fever
Athlete’s heart – symmetrical mild hypertrophy, normal LVOT gradient

ECG may be normal in early disease; do not exclude HOCM
